Finan PM.role: Biochemist and drug-discovery leader who started the PI 3-kinase drug discovery program at Novartis and ran its Developmental and Molecular Pathways group in Cambridge, Massachusetts, before moving into life-science venture investing
Finan PM.sub: Managing Partner, Epidarex Capital (partner since 2014) · Chairman, Enterprise Therapeutics · Global Head of Respiratory Disease Area and UK Site Head, Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research · Executive Director, Developmental and Molecular Pathways, Novartis (Cambridge, Massachusetts) · earlier at Cancer Research UK, Yamanouchi Research Institute and Karus Therapeutics · BSc and PhD in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, University of Leeds
story: Peter Finan is a co-author of two Atlas papers from a partnership between Brendan Manning's lab at Harvard and Novartis scientists in Cambridge, Massachusetts. DUV2010 asked what mTORC1, the growth-control complex, switches on besides protein synthesis. In mouse cells where mTORC1 is stuck in the on position (because the brake protein TSC2 is missing), the team measured thousands of genes and metabolites at once. mTORC1 turned on sugar breakdown (glycolysis), the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway and the building of new fats, through the transcription factors HIF1alpha and SREBP. DIB2012 found TBC1D7, a third core protein in the TSC1-TSC2 complex that acts as the brake on mTORC1. Both studies were done in cultured cells.

Finan studied biochemistry and molecular biology at the University of Leeds, where he also did his PhD. He worked at Cancer Research UK, the Yamanouchi Research Institute (now part of Astellas) and Karus Therapeutics, where he was Head of Biology. At Novartis he started the company's PI 3-kinase drug discovery program, which works on the signalling enzymes that sit just upstream of mTOR, and received the Novartis Leading Scientist Award in 2007. As Executive Director of the Developmental and Molecular Pathways platform in Cambridge, Massachusetts, he led target discovery and early drug discovery across cancer, neuroscience, regenerative medicine and inflammation. PubMed lists him at Novartis on papers from the same years on autophagy, rapamycin resistance and chemical tools for the autophagy enzyme VPS34. He later headed the Respiratory Disease Area and the Novartis research site in the UK.

Finan joined the life-science investor Epidarex Capital in 2014 and was named a Managing Partner in July 2026. He chairs Enterprise Therapeutics and sits on the boards of several young biotech companies and of the UK BioIndustry Association.

highlights.DIB2012: Co-author from the Novartis side of the Harvard-Novartis team that identified TBC1D7 as the third core subunit of the TSC1-TSC2 complex, the brake on mTORC1.
highlights.DUV2010: Co-author from Novartis on the study showing that active mTORC1 is enough to switch on glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway and fat synthesis in cultured cells.

Murphy LO.role: Cell biologist who led autophagy and mTOR drug discovery at Novartis in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and is now Chief Scientific Officer of Casma Therapeutics, a company that develops drugs acting on the autophagy-lysosome system
Murphy LO.sub: Chief Scientific Officer, Casma Therapeutics · Senior Vice President, Biology, Casma Therapeutics (from 2018) · Entrepreneur-in-residence, Third Rock Ventures · drug discovery group leader, Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts)
story: Leon Murphy is a co-author of two Atlas papers from Brendan Manning's Harvard lab and its Novartis collaborators. DUV2010 showed in cultured mouse cells that switching mTORC1, the growth-control complex, permanently on is enough to drive sugar breakdown, the pentose phosphate pathway and the making of new fats, through the transcription factors HIF1alpha and SREBP. DIB2012 added TBC1D7 as a third core part of the TSC1-TSC2 complex, the protein brake that keeps mTORC1 in check.

Murphy trained in biochemistry and cell biology. At the Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research in Cambridge, Massachusetts, he led a drug discovery group working on autophagy, the cell's system for breaking down and recycling its own parts, and on metabolic disease. PubMed shows his main line of work there: why rapamycin switches on autophagy in some cell lines but not others, and how combining it with a second kind of mTOR inhibitor overcomes this (2011); orally available inhibitors of the autophagy enzyme VPS34 (2015); and a CRISPR screen that found TMEM41B as a new autophagy gene (2018).

In 2018 Murphy moved to Third Rock Ventures as an entrepreneur-in-residence and helped found Casma Therapeutics, first as Senior Vice President of Biology and now as Chief Scientific Officer. With Noboru Mizushima he wrote a 2020 review on how to measure autophagy properly, and Casma's recent papers with academic groups study the lysosomal ion channel TRPML1 as a drug target.

Lebwohl D.role: Medical oncologist and drug developer who led the clinical development of everolimus (Afinitor) at Novartis through approvals in several cancers and tuberous sclerosis, and later served as Chief Medical Officer of the gene-editing company Intellia Therapeutics
Lebwohl D.sub: Executive Vice President and Chief Medical Officer, Intellia Therapeutics (2020–2026) · Chief Medical Officer, Semma Therapeutics (2018–2019) · Senior Vice President and Global Program Head, Novartis (everolimus, CAR-T and other programs) · Oncology Clinical Development, Bristol-Myers Squibb · MD, Yale University School of Medicine · AB in Biochemical Sciences, Harvard College
story: David Lebwohl appears on five Atlas papers, all large clinical trials of everolimus, a rapamycin-like drug that blocks mTORC1, the growth-control complex. RECORD-1 (MOT2008) tested it in advanced kidney cancer, BOLERO-2 (BAS2012) in hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer together with exemestane, and RADIANT-3 (YAO2011) in pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours. EXIST-1 (FRA2013) and EXIST-2 (BIS2013) tested it in tuberous sclerosis complex, a genetic disease in which the TSC genes that normally hold mTORC1 back are broken, causing brain tumours called SEGAs and kidney tumours called angiomyolipomas. These are studies in patients, and they are much of the reason everolimus is an approved medicine today.

Lebwohl studied biochemical sciences at Harvard College and medicine at Yale. He did his internal medicine residency at Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston and a fellowship at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, and is board certified in internal medicine and hematology. He spent about five years in oncology clinical development at Bristol-Myers Squibb before joining Novartis.

At Novartis he led global drug programs. Under his leadership Afinitor (everolimus) was approved for five indications, including breast, kidney, brain and lung tumours, and he later led development of the CAR-T cell therapy Kymriah and the company's Cell and Gene Therapies Unit. In 2018 he became Chief Medical Officer of Semma Therapeutics, which worked on stem-cell-derived insulin-making cells for type 1 diabetes, and in 2020 Chief Medical Officer of Intellia Therapeutics, a CRISPR gene-editing company. Intellia announced in August 2025 that he would retire on 7 August 2026.

story: Tarek Sahmoud is a Novartis co-author of three Atlas trials of everolimus, a rapamycin-like drug that blocks mTORC1, the growth-control complex. BOLERO-2 (BAS2012) added everolimus to the hormone drug exemestane in women with advanced hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer whose disease had grown on earlier hormone treatment. EXIST-1 (FRA2013) and EXIST-2 (BIS2013) tested everolimus in tuberous sclerosis complex, a genetic disease in which mTORC1 runs unchecked and benign tumours grow in the brain and kidneys. These are randomised trials in patients, and they supported approval of everolimus for these uses.

Sahmoud qualified in medicine at Cairo University in Egypt and earned a PhD in public health, epidemiology and biostatistics at the University of Bordeaux II in France. He coordinated clinical trials for several disease groups at the EORTC, the European cancer trials organisation, and worked in drug development at AstraZeneca, Bristol-Myers Squibb and Boehringer Ingelheim. At Novartis he was Vice President and Senior Global Clinical Program Head in oncology drug development, the role he held when these trials were reported.

He then became Corporate Vice President and Global Head of Clinical Development in solid tumours and immuno-oncology at Celgene, Chief Medical Officer of H3 Biomedicine in Cambridge, Massachusetts in 2016, and Chief Medical Officer of Humanigen in 2018. A current position could not be confirmed.

Deleu I.role: Medical oncologist at the AZ Nikolaas hospital in Sint-Niklaas, Belgium, who enrolled patients in international breast cancer drug trials, including the BOLERO-2 trial of everolimus
Deleu I.sub: Medical oncologist, Oncologic Centre, AZ Nikolaas, Sint-Niklaas, Belgium (affiliation on PubMed papers from 2011 to 2022)
story: Ines Deleu is a co-author of the two Atlas reports from BOLERO-2, a large trial in postmenopausal women with advanced breast cancer that is driven by hormones (hormone-receptor-positive) and does not carry extra copies of the HER2 gene. These cancers often learn to grow despite hormone treatment, and switching on the mTOR pathway is one way they do it. BOLERO-2 added everolimus, a rapamycin-like drug that blocks mTORC1, the growth-control complex, to the hormone drug exemestane. The first report (BAS2012) showed that the combination kept the cancer from growing for several months longer than exemestane alone. The final report (PIC2014) found that this gain held up, but that overall survival was not significantly longer (31.0 against 26.6 months).

Large cancer trials like this one run at hundreds of hospitals, and site investigators enrol and treat the patients, collect the data and sign off on the final paper. PubMed lists Deleu at AZ Nikolaas, a general hospital in Sint-Niklaas in Flanders, on about a dozen papers, most of them multicentre breast cancer trials. The most recent, from 2022, is the phase III EMERALD trial of elacestrant, an oral drug that breaks down the estrogen receptor.
No official profile page could be checked for this profile, so details of training and the current position beyond the PubMed affiliation are not given here.

highlights.BAS2012: Site investigator and co-author at AZ Nikolaas on BOLERO-2, the trial that added everolimus to exemestane in advanced hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer.
highlights.PIC2014: Co-author of the final BOLERO-2 report, which confirmed the gain in progression-free survival but found no significant gain in overall survival.

Castilho RM.role: Dentist and cell biologist who showed, as a postdoc at the US National Institutes of Health, that Wnt signalling wears out skin stem cells through mTOR and that rapamycin can prevent it, and whose University of Michigan lab now studies how histone marks control epithelial healing and treatment resistance in head and neck cancer
Castilho RM.sub: Professor of Dentistry (promotion recommended 2024), Associate Professor with tenure (2018–2024) and Assistant Professor (2010–2018), Department of Periodontics and Oral Medicine, School of Dentistry, University of Michigan · postdoctoral fellow, National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research, NIH (about seven years) · PhD (2003) and MS (2000), University of Sao Paulo · DDS, Pontifical Catholic University of Campinas (1995)
story: In the Atlas paper (CAS2009), Rogerio Castilho and colleagues in J. Silvio Gutkind's group at the US National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research looked at the stem cells that renew the skin and hair. They kept the Wnt signal, which tells these stem cells to divide, switched on in mice. At first the hair grew fast, but soon the stem cells stopped working, became senescent (a state where cells stop dividing for good) and the hair was lost. The cause was mTOR: Wnt kept mTOR active, and when the mice were given rapamycin, which blocks mTOR, the stem cells kept going. The study is in mice and in cultured cells, and it helped connect mTOR to the way stem cells run out with age.

Castilho trained as a dentist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Campinas in Brazil (DDS 1995) and earned an MS and a PhD in oral pathology at the University of Sao Paulo (2003), where he also taught surgical and experimental pathology. He then spent nearly seven years as a postdoctoral fellow at the NIDCR, part of the National Institutes of Health, studying how the lining of the mouth and skin stays healthy, heals wounds and turns into cancer.

He joined the University of Michigan School of Dentistry in 2010 and was recommended for promotion to full professor in 2024. His lab studies the histone code, the chemical marks on the proteins that package DNA, in tissue injury, chronic inflammation and cancer. It asks how histone acetylation controls healing and stem cell function, and how head and neck tumours, including salivary gland cancers, use these marks to resist chemotherapy and radiation. The group also tests drugs that change these marks, and works on better healing of burns.

highlights.CAS2009: First author: showed in mice that constant Wnt signalling exhausts epidermal stem cells through mTOR and that rapamycin prevents this stem cell loss.

Quinn D.role: Clinical trial investigator at P3 Research in Wellington, New Zealand, who was a co-author of the resTORbio trials that tested low-dose mTOR inhibitors to strengthen immunity in older adults
Quinn D.sub: P3 Research, Newtown, Wellington, New Zealand (affiliation on PubMed papers) · listed with resTORbio, Boston, on the 2021 trial report
story: Dean Quinn is a co-author of two Atlas papers on whether short, low-dose courses of mTOR-blocking drugs can make older people's immune systems work better. In MAN2018, a phase 2a trial in 264 older adults, six weeks of a low-dose combination of BEZ235 and everolimus was followed by fewer reported infections over the next year, more active antiviral genes and a better response to the flu vaccine. MAN2021 then tested BEZ235 alone (renamed RTB101) in two bigger trials. The phase 2b trial (652 people) showed fewer lab-confirmed respiratory infections only in an analysis that was not corrected for multiple testing, and the phase 3 trial (1,024 people) found no difference in its main endpoint. Taken together, these are human trials that gave an early signal and then a negative confirmatory result, a useful lesson in how drug evidence develops.

Trials like these recruit volunteers at specialised research clinics. PubMed lists Quinn at P3 Research in Newtown, Wellington, a clinical trials company in New Zealand, on about ten trial reports, and the 2021 paper also lists him with resTORbio, the Boston company that ran the RTB101 program.
No official profile was found to confirm Quinn's medical training or current position, so this profile is limited to what the publications show.

highlights.MAN2018: Trial investigator and co-author on the phase 2a study linking a short low-dose course of BEZ235 plus everolimus with fewer infections in older adults.
highlights.MAN2021: Co-author, listed with resTORbio and P3 Research, on the phase 2b and phase 3 trials of RTB101, where the phase 3 trial did not confirm a clinical benefit.

story: Amany Ahmed is the senior (last) author of HAFEZ2026, a mouse study of psoriasis, the skin disease with thick, red, scaly patches. The team caused psoriasis-like skin disease in mice with imiquimod cream and then gave melittin, the main peptide in bee venom. Melittin reduced the severity of the skin disease by about 60 percent. In the treated skin the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway was turned down and autophagy, the cell's recycling system, was turned up. This is a mouse study at a high injected dose, so it shows a mechanism worth testing, not a treatment for people.

PubMed lists Ahmed at the Pharmacology and Toxicology Department of Helwan University's Faculty of Pharmacy on about 25 papers since 2020, usually as senior author. The studies follow a common plan: a disease is induced in rats or mice and a drug or plant compound is tested for protection. Examples include the diabetes drug lixisenatide in a rat model of stroke (2020), the weight-loss drug semaglutide in a rat model of osteoporosis after loss of the ovaries (2024), and the plant compound phloridzin against lung scarring caused by the cancer drug bleomycin (2026), where autophagy was again one of the processes measured.
No university profile could be checked, so academic rank and training are not given here.

highlights.HAFEZ2026: Senior author: showed in mice that melittin from bee venom eases psoriasis-like skin disease while lowering PI3K/Akt/mTOR signalling and raising autophagy.

Landoas A.lab_name: Pharmacy Department, Grenoble Alpes University Hospital, Universite Grenoble Alpes (Grenoble, France)
Landoas A.role: Hospital pharmacist at Grenoble Alpes University Hospital who studies how everolimus is used after lung transplantation and whether it protects the new lungs from long-term rejection
Landoas A.sub: Pharmacy Department, Grenoble Alpes University Hospital and Universite Grenoble Alpes, France (affiliation on PubMed papers from 2021 to 2026)
story: Agathe Landoas is the first author of LANDOAS2026, a study of people who had received a lung transplant. The biggest long-term threat to a transplanted lung is chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD), a slow scarring and narrowing of the airways caused largely by the immune system. Everolimus, a drug that blocks mTOR and calms immune cells, is often added to the standard anti-rejection drugs, mainly to spare the kidneys. Landoas and colleagues looked back at the records of patients treated in Grenoble and asked whether the timing and continuity of everolimus mattered. Starting it later and stopping and restarting it more often were both linked to a higher risk of CLAD. Because this was a retrospective, single-hospital study, it shows an association and not proof that early, steady everolimus prevents CLAD.

The paper follows an earlier study from the same Grenoble team, with Landoas as first author (2024), which compared 59 lung transplant patients who received everolimus on top of standard treatment with 37 who did not. CLAD was less frequent and came later in the everolimus group. PubMed lists Landoas at the Pharmacy Department of Grenoble Alpes University Hospital on five papers since 2021, including a French nursing-journal article on insulin with the hospital pharmacy team, and with Pierrick Bedouch, a professor of clinical pharmacy, as senior author on the transplant work.
No official profile was available, so training and current position beyond the PubMed affiliation are not given.

highlights.LANDOAS2026: First author: in a retrospective single-centre study of lung transplant patients, later start and more interruptions of everolimus were linked to a higher risk of chronic lung allograft dysfunction.

Lovat P.lab_name: Translational and Clinical Research Institute, Newcastle University (Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom)
Lovat P.role: Newcastle University cancer biologist who studies autophagy in melanoma and whose work on the autophagy protein AMBRA1 and the skin protein loricrin underlies a test, developed with AMLo Biosciences, to identify early melanomas at low risk of spreading
Lovat P.sub: Translational and Clinical Research Institute and Newcastle University Centre for Cancer, Newcastle University · AMLo Biosciences Ltd, Newcastle upon Tyne
story: Penny Lovat is a co-author of two Atlas papers from Viktor Korolchuk's lab at Newcastle University on why ageing cells behave as they do. CAR2017 showed that in senescent human cells (cells that have permanently stopped dividing) mTORC1, the growth-control complex, stays switched on even when nutrients or growth factors are taken away. The fault lies upstream, in how the cells sense amino acids and growth signals, and the cells come to depend on this signal to survive. KEL2024 showed that healthy human cells constantly recycle damaged mitochondria (basal mitophagy), that this stops when cells become senescent, and that part of rapamycin's anti-ageing effect on cells needs mitophagy to be restored. Both studies were done in cultured human cells.

Lovat's own research centres on autophagy, the cell's recycling system, in skin cancer. PubMed lists her at Newcastle University on more than 50 papers on melanoma and autophagy. Her group found that the autophagy regulator AMBRA1 and the skin barrier protein loricrin are lost from the skin above melanomas that are more likely to spread. With collaborators in Rome she showed that the HPV virus breaks down AMBRA1 in throat cancers, which lowers autophagy and makes the tumour cells easier to kill with cisplatin (2020). A 2026 study tested AMBRA1 and loricrin staining to help pathologists tell high-grade moles from thin melanomas.

PubMed papers list Lovat both at Newcastle University's Translational and Clinical Research Institute and at AMLo Biosciences, the Newcastle company that brings the AMBRA1 and loricrin test to clinical use. Details of training and academic title could not be confirmed from an official page.

highlights.CAR2017: Co-author on the Newcastle study showing that senescent human cells keep mTORC1 switched on because their sensing of amino acids and growth factors is broken.
highlights.KEL2024: Co-author on the study showing that loss of basal mitophagy drives cellular ageing and that rapamycin's anti-senescence effect depends on restoring it.

O'Reilly KE.lab_name: Department of Dermatology, New York University School of Medicine (New York, New York, USA)
O'Reilly KE.role: Physician-scientist who, in Neal Rosen's lab at Memorial Sloan Kettering, showed that blocking mTORC1 with rapamycin-like drugs switches on the survival kinase Akt through a feedback loop, a main reason these drugs worked less well against cancer than hoped
O'Reilly KE.sub: Department of Dermatology, New York University School of Medicine (2009, at the time of the most recent PubMed paper) · Program in Molecular Pharmacology and Chemistry, Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center, Neal Rosen lab (2006)
story: Kathryn O'Reilly is the first author of ORE2006, one of the most cited papers on why rapamycin-like drugs disappointed as cancer treatments. Normally, when mTORC1 and its target S6K1 are active, they send a brake signal back up the pathway that dampens insulin and growth-factor receptors. O'Reilly and colleagues in Neal Rosen's lab showed that blocking mTORC1 takes that brake off. Signals from receptor tyrosine kinases then rise, and Akt, a kinase that helps cancer cells survive, becomes more active. They saw this in cancer cell lines and also in tumour samples from patients treated with everolimus (RAD001), so it is a real effect in people, not only in a dish. The finding pushed the field toward drugs that block both mTOR and the PI3K/Akt pathway, or mTOR together with growth-factor receptors.

PubMed lists O'Reilly on 11 papers. In 2009, at the Department of Dermatology of New York University School of Medicine and again with Neal Rosen among the co-authors, she was first author of a study of 72 patients with metastatic melanoma, which found that a high level of phosphorylated 4E-BP1, a sign that mTORC1 is driving protein synthesis, went with shorter survival.
A current position could not be confirmed, and the most recent confirmed affiliation (NYU, 2009) is given at the time of that study.

highlights.ORE2006: First author: showed in cancer cells and in patient tumours treated with everolimus that mTORC1 inhibition removes a feedback brake and activates upstream receptor signalling and Akt.

story: Trevor Stitt is a co-author of two 2001 Atlas papers from Regeneron that made mTOR central to muscle biology. BOD2001 showed in living mice and rats that switching on Akt makes muscle fibres grow larger, that blocking mTOR with rapamycin stops this growth, and that active Akt can protect muscle from wasting (atrophy). ROM2001 showed in cultured muscle cells (myotubes) that the growth signal IGF-1 enlarges muscle cells through Akt and two branches below it, mTOR and GSK3. Together these papers explain why mTOR is the main switch linking growth signals and exercise to muscle size.

PubMed lists Stitt at Regeneron Pharmaceuticals in Tarrytown, New York, on 23 papers. The earlier ones come from Regeneron's work on growth factors and their receptors in the nervous system. In 1995, as first author in Cell, Stitt reported that the blood-clotting regulator protein S and the related protein Gas6 are the ligands for the Tyro3 and Axl receptor tyrosine kinases. Later papers stay with the muscle program led by David Glass, including a 2004 paper on how IGF-1 and Akt block the switching on of the atrophy enzymes MuRF1 and MAFbx, and a 2007 paper showing that MuRF1 breaks down myosin heavy chain, the main motor protein of muscle.
No official profile was found, so training and current position are not given.

highlights.BOD2001: Co-author on the in vivo study showing that Akt/mTOR signalling drives skeletal muscle hypertrophy and can prevent muscle atrophy.
highlights.ROM2001: Co-author on the cultured-myotube study showing that IGF-1 grows muscle cells through Akt and both its mTOR and GSK3 branches.

Tao J.lab_name: Research Centre of Environmental Ecology and Fish Nutrition, College of Fisheries and Life Science, Shanghai Ocean University (Shanghai, China)
Tao J.role: Fish nutrition researcher at Shanghai Ocean University who studies why carnivorous farmed fish such as largemouth bass handle dietary carbohydrate poorly and how this links to mTOR signalling in the liver
Tao J.sub: Research Centre of Environmental Ecology and Fish Nutrition, Shanghai Ocean University (affiliation on PubMed papers from 2023 to 2026)
story: Jiajie Tao is the first author of TAO2026, a study in largemouth bass, a meat-eating fish that is farmed widely in China. Fish feed is cheaper when it contains more starch, but carnivorous fish cope badly with it: their livers fill up with glycogen, the stored form of sugar, much like animals with glucose intolerance. The study asked why. It found that in the bass liver the insulin-responsive mTOR/SREBP1 pathway, which normally turns extra sugar into fat, works poorly. When this route is impaired, more of the sugar ends up stored as glycogen. The work is in fish, so it tells us about how mTOR helps decide where sugar goes in the liver, not directly about people.

PubMed lists Tao at Shanghai Ocean University's Research Centre on Environmental Ecology and Fish Nutrition on about a dozen papers since 2023, most of them on carbohydrate use in largemouth bass, usually with Songlin Li as senior author. An earlier first-author paper (2023) showed that adding cultures of the gut bacterium Clostridium butyricum to a high-starch diet reduced glycogen build-up in the bass liver and raised insulin-signalling and glycolysis genes.
No official profile was found, so training and position are given only from the publication record.

highlights.TAO2026: First author: showed in largemouth bass that weak insulin-driven mTOR/SREBP1 fat synthesis in the liver goes with glycogen overload on high-carbohydrate feed.

Li S.lab_name: Research Centre of Environmental Ecology and Fish Nutrition, College of Fisheries and Life Science, Shanghai Ocean University (Shanghai, China)
Li S.role: Fish nutrition scientist at Shanghai Ocean University who leads research on how largemouth bass and other farmed fish use carbohydrate and other nutrients in their feed
Li S.sub: Research Centre of Environmental Ecology and Fish Nutrition and National Demonstration Center on Experiment Teaching of Fisheries Science, Shanghai Ocean University
story: Songlin Li is the senior (last) author of TAO2026, which studied why largemouth bass, a carnivorous farmed fish, store too much glycogen in the liver when fed starch-rich feed. The team found that the liver's insulin-responsive mTOR/SREBP1 pathway, which would normally turn surplus sugar into fat, is impaired in this fish, so sugar is stored as glycogen instead. The result is from fish, and it adds a comparative view of how mTOR helps share out sugar between storage forms in the liver.

PubMed lists Li at Shanghai Ocean University's Research Centre on Environmental Ecology and Fish Nutrition, and at the university's National Demonstration Center on Experiment Teaching of Fisheries Science, as senior author of more than 30 papers on largemouth bass nutrition. The work tests feed ingredients and additives, such as the gut bacterium Clostridium butyricum (2023), to help fish cope with high-carbohydrate diets, and measures liver metabolism, antioxidant defences and gut bacteria.

Because Li is a very common Chinese surname, only papers with the Shanghai Ocean University fish-nutrition affiliation were counted. No official profile could be checked, so academic rank and training are not given.

Hakkola J.lab_name: Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, Pharmacology and Toxicology, University of Oulu (Oulu, Finland)
Hakkola J.role: Pharmacologist at the University of Oulu who studies the pregnane X receptor (PXR), a liver sensor of drugs and foreign chemicals, and how it changes liver growth and metabolism
Hakkola J.sub: Pharmacology and Toxicology, Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, Biocenter Oulu and Medical Research Center Oulu, University of Oulu and Oulu University Hospital
story: Jukka Hakkola is the senior author of LASSILA2026, a study that joins a small clinical trial with mouse work. The pregnane X receptor (PXR) is a protein in liver cells that detects many drugs and chemicals and switches on genes to deal with them. Rifampicin, an antibiotic, activates it strongly. In 16 healthy volunteers, one week of rifampicin made the liver about 2.7 percent larger relative to body weight. In male mice, activating PXR also enlarged the liver, and this came with higher activity of the AKT-MTOR growth pathway but not of YAP, another known driver of liver growth. The human part shows the effect is real in people, while the mTOR link comes from the mice.

Hakkola has worked on PXR for many years. PubMed lists him on more than 25 PXR papers from the University of Oulu, usually as senior author. A 2025 study from the group, for example, found Lasp2, a small cell-adhesion protein, as a new PXR target gene in mouse liver, with partners at Charles University in Hradec Kralove, Czech Republic. The wider theme is how drug-sensing receptors in the liver also change glucose and fat metabolism and the size of the organ.

He leads the pharmacology and toxicology group in the Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine at the University of Oulu, which is linked with Biocenter Oulu and Oulu University Hospital. His academic title and training could not be confirmed from an official page.

highlights.LASSILA2026: Senior author: led the trial showing that a week of rifampicin enlarges the human liver and the mouse work tying PXR-driven liver growth to AKT-MTOR signalling.

Yang YC.role: Scientist at Revolution Medicines who worked on the company's bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitors, from the breast cancer lab studies of RMC-6272 to the first trial of RMC-5552 in patients
Yang YC.sub: Revolution Medicines, Redwood City, California (affiliation on PubMed papers from 2023 to 2026)
story: Yu Chi Yang is a co-author of two Atlas papers on a new kind of mTOR drug. Rapamycin and its relatives only partly block mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and leave one of its key targets, 4E-BP1, largely untouched. Drugs that block the mTOR enzyme site block mTORC1 fully but also hit mTORC2, which causes side effects such as high blood sugar. Revolution Medicines built bi-steric molecules, which join a rapamycin-like part to an enzyme-site part so that they bind two places at once and prefer mTORC1. MEN2023 showed that one of them, RMC-6272, fully shut down mTORC1, including 4E-BP1, and overcame resistance to hormone therapy and CDK4/6 inhibitors in breast cancer cells and in tumours from patients grown in mice. SCH2025 was the first trial of the related drug RMC-5552 in 57 patients with advanced solid tumours. High blood sugar was uncommon (4 percent) and the disease was controlled in 64 percent of patients, but with no comparison group the trial cannot prove that sparing mTORC2 is the reason.
PubMed lists Yang at Revolution Medicines in Redwood City, California, on 17 papers from 2023 to 2026, in the company's work on targeted cancer drugs.
Because Yang is a very common surname, only papers with the Revolution Medicines affiliation were counted. No official profile was found, so training and job title are not given.

highlights.MEN2023: Revolution Medicines co-author on the preclinical study showing that the bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitor RMC-6272 overcomes drug resistance in breast cancer models.

Ikeno Y.lab_name: Sam and Ann Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Ikeno Y.role: Pathologist at the Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies in San Antonio whose examinations of tissues from aged mice help ageing studies tell whether an intervention changes disease, especially cancer, late in life
Ikeno Y.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (affiliation on PubMed papers)
story: Yuji Ikeno is a co-author of two Atlas papers on ageing. LAB2015, from Judith Campisi's group, studied senescent cells, old cells that stop dividing but keep releasing inflammatory signals called the SASP. These signals can harm nearby tissue and even help tumours grow. The team showed that mTOR drives the SASP by boosting the production of IL1A, the signal at the top of the cascade, and that rapamycin turned this off and stopped senescent cells from feeding prostate tumour growth in mice. DUR2026, from John Kopchick's group, deleted the growth hormone receptor in mice at 12 months of age, which is middle age for a mouse. The mice still lived longer, in both sexes, and the males kept better insulin sensitivity, muscle performance and bone. This matters because most growth-hormone longevity mice lack the hormone signal from birth, while this study shows that a midlife start is still enough.

PubMed lists Ikeno on more than 120 papers on ageing, many of them from the Barshop Institute in San Antonio, where the long-lived mouse models and anti-ageing drug studies need careful pathology to show what the animals died of and which diseases were delayed. In both Atlas papers the role is consistent with this: examining tissues from the mice.
No official profile could be checked, so academic rank and training are not given here.

highlights.LAB2015: Co-author on the study showing that mTOR drives the senescence-associated secretory phenotype through IL1A translation and that rapamycin blocks it.
highlights.DUR2026: Co-author on the study showing that deleting the growth hormone receptor in midlife still extends healthy lifespan in mice.

Burris HA.lab_name: Sarah Cannon Research Institute (Nashville, Tennessee, USA)

story: Howard Burris is a co-author of two Atlas trial papers about mTOR drugs in cancer. PIC2014 is the final report of BOLERO-2, which added everolimus, a rapamycin-like mTORC1 blocker, to the hormone drug exemestane in women with advanced hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer. The combination kept the cancer in check for longer (7.8 against 3.2 months) but did not significantly lengthen overall survival. SCH2025 was the first trial in patients of RMC-5552, a newer bi-steric drug designed to block mTORC1 fully while sparing mTORC2. In 57 patients with advanced solid tumours, high blood sugar, a typical side effect of older mTOR drugs, was uncommon (4 percent). Without a comparison group, the trial is an early signal, not proof.

Burris works at the Sarah Cannon Research Institute in Nashville, one of the largest centres in the United States for early-phase (phase 1) cancer trials, where new drugs are first given to patients to find a safe dose. PubMed lists him with a Sarah Cannon affiliation on more than 200 trial papers, which shows how many new cancer drugs pass through this kind of centre on the way to approval.
No official profile could be checked, so title, training and leadership roles are not given here.

Nazemi M.lab_name: Rainero Lab, School of Biosciences, University of Sheffield (Sheffield, England, United Kingdom)
Nazemi M.role: Cell biologist in Elena Rainero's lab at the University of Sheffield who studies how the collagen-rich matrix around tumours feeds cancer cells when nutrients run short
Nazemi M.sub: School of Biosciences, University of Sheffield, Elena Rainero lab (affiliation on PubMed papers from 2020 to 2026)
story: Mona Nazemi is the first author of NAZ2026. Breast and pancreatic tumours are packed in collagen I, the main protein of scar-like tissue, and the blood supply in them is poor, so cancer cells are often short of amino acids. The study found that cancer cells sitting on collagen I use their collagen receptor, alpha2beta1 integrin, to switch on mTORC1 and its target S6, and to bring the amino acid transporter LAT1-4F2hc to the cell surface. More transporter at the surface means more essential amino acids get in, and the cells survive. In patient data, high LAT1-4F2hc levels in basal-like breast and pancreatic tumours went with a worse outlook. This links the tumour's surroundings directly to mTORC1, the cell's nutrient sensor.

Nazemi has worked with Elena Rainero at Sheffield since at least 2020, when they wrote a review on how the tumour matrix and cell metabolism talk to each other. In a 2024 PLoS Biology paper, also as first author, Nazemi showed that invasive breast cancer cells starved of amino acids can swallow pieces of the surrounding matrix, break them down in lysosomes and use the released tyrosine and phenylalanine to keep growing.
No official profile was found, so training and current role are given only from the publication record.

highlights.NAZ2026: First author: showed that collagen I activates mTORC1/S6 and brings the LAT1-4F2hc amino acid transporter to the cell surface, helping cancer cells survive nutrient shortage.

Li R.lab_name: Hubei Key Laboratory of Genetic Regulation and Integrative Biology, School of Life Sciences, Central China Normal University (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
Li R.role: Toxicologist at Central China Normal University in Wuhan who leads mouse studies of how early-life exposure to microplastics, nanoplastics and plastic additives harms the developing brain
Li R.sub: Key Laboratory of Pesticide and Chemical Biology of the Ministry of Education and Hubei Key Laboratory of Genetic Regulation and Integrative Biology, School of Life Sciences, Central China Normal University
story: Rui Li is the senior (last) author of YANG2026. Young children take in tiny plastic particles from bottles, toys and food containers, often together with DEHP, a chemical that makes plastic soft. In this study, young mice exposed to polypropylene microplastics and DEHP developed brain and behaviour changes that resemble features of autism spectrum disorder, including reduced social behaviour. In their brains mTOR was overactive and autophagy, the cell's recycling system that mTOR normally restrains, was impaired. Treating the mice with rapamycin restored autophagy and improved the social and behavioural problems. The work is in mice, so it shows a possible mechanism, not proof that plastic exposure causes autism in children.

PubMed lists Li as senior author of a series of papers from the School of Life Sciences at Central China Normal University on plastic pollution and the young brain. In 2023 the group reported that combined exposure to polypropylene microplastics and DEHP caused memory problems, damage in the hippocampus and inflammation in young mice, through a long-lasting stress response in the protein-folding system. In 2025, in ACS Nano, the group showed that polystyrene nanoplastics disturb protein balance in the brain partly through changes in gut bacteria, with the sugar trehalose acting as a link between gut and brain.
Because Li is a very common surname, only papers from this Central China Normal University group were counted. No official profile could be checked, so academic rank and training are not given.

highlights.YANG2026: Senior author: led the mouse study linking early-life microplastic and DEHP exposure to mTOR overactivity, impaired autophagy and autism-like behaviour, which rapamycin reversed.

story: Jian Yin is the first author of YIN2026, a structural study of PAT1 (also called SLC36A1), a human transporter that carries small amino acids across membranes together with protons. Earlier work by other groups had shown that PAT1 sits on lysosomes, the cell's recycling compartments, and helps move amino acids out of them, which affects how mTORC1, the cell's nutrient sensor, is switched on. Yin and colleagues used cryo-electron microscopy, a method that freezes proteins and images them with electrons, to see PAT1 empty and with different amino acids bound. The structures show that the transporter grips many different amino acids in a similar way. The study is about the shape and mechanism of the protein; the mTORC1 link comes from the earlier work.

Lv N.lab_name: School of Medicine, Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine (Nanjing, China)
Lv N.role: Researcher at Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine who led a mouse study showing that the age-related loss of Lamtor5, a part of the lysosomal platform that helps switch on mTORC1, drives immune ageing through inflammation
Lv N.sub: School of Medicine, Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Nianyin Lv is the first author of LV2026. mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, is switched on at the surface of lysosomes, with the help of a protein complex called the Ragulator (LAMTOR1 to LAMTOR5) that anchors the docking machinery there. The study found that one of these proteins, Lamtor5, falls with age in macrophages, the immune cells that eat debris and germs. When Lamtor5 is lost, macrophages age early and release signals through the cGAS-STING pathway, a DNA-sensing alarm system, that spread inflammation to other tissues and push the whole body toward ageing. Putting Lamtor5 back into old mice reversed the immune ageing and eased other ageing signs. The work is in mice and gives a link between lysosomes, mTOR signalling and inflammation in old age.

PubMed shows other papers under the same initials at Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine, but they could not be tied to this researcher with confidence, so they are not used here. No official profile was found, so training and current position are not given.
